docs.title: CanaryBit Confidential Cloud
docs.text:
Confidential Cloud is a suite of advanced security solutions developed by CanaryBit, designed to provide Enterprises and the Public Sector with robust tools for infrastructure and AI security.

The cross-industry tools are particularly valuable for organisations in mission-critical domains and critical infrastructure, such as Finance, Healthcare, Energy, Digital Infrastructure, Defence and more. Organizations using Confidential Cloud can finally guarantee end-to-end data protection by immediately detecting faulty execution environments that do not meet custom security requirements, and maintain compliance with industry-specific regulatory requirements.

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
This section contains practical hardening guidance for AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX Confidential Computing deployments. The documents are separated by platform and by host/guest responsibility so operators can find the relevant steps quickly.

Recommended order

  1. Select the platform guide: SEV-SNP or TDX.
  2. Review the host guide with the platform or infrastructure operator.
  3. Review the guest guide with the image and workload owner.
  4. Agree on required configuration and attestation claims before deploying workloads.
  5. Validate the deployed platform and guest state using current vendor documentation and attestation tooling.

Warning

Some controls are set by the host or at guest launch and cannot be changed from inside a running guest. Coordinate host-side changes with the infrastructure owner.

Info

Treat attestation as a verification step: define which measurements, policy fields, TCB levels, and freshness requirements the relying party must accept.

A successful boot alone does not prove that the intended hardening policy is active.

docs.text:
• Host hardening: firmware and host software updates, kernel and QEMU support, and restricted-injection host requirements.
  • Guest hardening: guest policy, PMC and page-movement restrictions, restricted injection requirements, guest identity, and attestation validation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Industries across the globe are increasingly recognizing that AI and data analytics are no longer optional add-ons but essential drivers of competitiveness and growth.

With the explosion of digital information, businesses face the challenge of extracting meaningful insights from massive datasets, something traditional methods simply cannot handle efficiently.

AI-powered analytics enables organizations to predict consumer behavior, optimize supply chains, detect fraud, personalize customer experiences, and streamline operations with unprecedented accuracy and speed. In sectors like Aerospace & Defence, Healthcare, Finance, Energy, the ability to harness data through AI is directly tied to innovation, cost savings, and long-term sustainability. In short, industries that fail to embrace AI and data analytics risk falling behind in a marketplace that increasingly rewards agility, intelligence, and data-driven decision-making.

However, while AI and data analytics offer enormous potential, they also carry significant risks that industries must carefully manage:

  • Security & Privacy
  • Compliance
  • Legal & IP
  • Liability & Reputational
  • Societal

CanaryBit Confidential Cloud helps mitigate relevant risks ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability of sensitive digital assets.

docs.title: 2. Deploy your Confidential environment with CanaryBit Tower
docs.text:
CanaryBit Tower comes with a set of examples that can be used to provision a secure environment in your target infrastructure.

Download CanaryBit Tower configuration for Public Cloud deployments and use the example file related to your target infrastructure.

Finally, deploy the environment following the steps documented in the Products :: TOWER page.

docs.title: 3. Get your environment verified by CanaryBit Inspector
docs.text:
The verification of your Confidential environment is triggered automatically when using CanaryBit Tower.

Optional: Manual verification

If manual verification is preferred, you would need to upload the CanaryBit (cb-inspector-client) agent on each Confidential VM you would like to attest.

Specifically, you would need to:

  1. Install the CanaryBit (cb) CLI tool

  2. Authenticate and retrieve your CanaryBit Inspector token ($CBTOKEN): 

    cb login cbinspector
    The returned temporary token will be used by cb-inspector-client to communicate with CanaryBit Inspector.

  3. Download the cb-inspector-client: 

    ./cb download cb-inspector-client

  4. Copy the cb-inspector-client on each Confidential VM.

  5. From each Confidential VM, run: 

    cb-inspector-client --token $CBTOKEN --environments $HW_ENV --inspector-url https://api.inspector.confidentialcloud.io
    providing $CBTOKEN and $HW_ENV ("snp" or "tdx", depending on your hardware chipset) as arguments.

docs.title: AMD SEV-SNP Guest Hardening
docs.text: This guide covers the guest-side hardening decisions for AMD SEV-SNP confidential VMs. It focuses on the settings a guest owner must verify and the runtime checks needed to confirm the guest is launched in a hardened policy.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
The guest should boot with the minimum trusted surface and a policy that blocks unsafe features and host-controlled behaviors.

The key principles are:

  • keep the guest policy restrictive
  • avoid enabling PMC virtualization
  • Keep the guest kernel updated
  • ensure the guest is built with SNP-aware firmware and kernel support
  • validate the attestation report before the VM is accepted

docs.title: 2. Verify the guest stack supports SNP
2.1 Check the guest firmware/kernel environment
docs.text:
The guest should use SNP-aware firmware and an SNP-aware Linux guest kernel. For upstream Linux, 6.11 is a baseline for SEV-SNP guest support; distributions may backport that support to earlier kernels. Treat the vendor-supported kernel release and verified SNP capabilities as authoritative, rather than relying on the version number alone. Optional features such as restricted injection may require additional, version-specific patches.

uname -a
cat /proc/cmdline

uname -a reports the running kernel release, build, and system architecture. /proc/cmdline reports the boot parameters actually passed to the running guest; it does not show the kernel version or prove that the kernel supports a feature.

If the guest is a cloud VM or custom image, verify the image includes the expected SNP support. Use the cloud or image-management update process to install a vendor-supported kernel, then verify the active kernel and its SNP capabilities.

docs.title: 3. Prevent PMC virtualization
docs.text:
PMC means performance monitoring counters. These are specialized hardware registers inside AMD CPUs (core PMCs, L3/uncore PMCs, Data Fabric PMCs, etc.) that count low-level processor events such as:

  • Retired instructions
  • Retired branches / taken branches
  • Cache accesses/misses
  • Division operations and cycles
  • And hundreds of other micro-architectural events

AMD EPYC generations (notably the 8005 series and beyond) added PMC Virtualization / Guest PMC Event Filtering. This allows:

  • Hardware filtering of which events a guest is allowed to program
  • Better isolation so the host cannot freely observe guest performance-counter activity.

In the AMD SEV-SNP Firmware ABI Specification (Publication 56860), SEV_FEATURES[11] is VIRT_PERFMON (virtualized performance monitoring). Use the ABI revision applicable to the platform when interpreting this and other feature bits.

docs.title: 3.1 Security requirement of PMC virtualization
docs.text:
Do not enable VIRT_PERFMON (SEV_FEATURES[11]) at launch.

This is the guest-side equivalent of a host policy decision and is essential for limiting performance-counter attacks.

If the guest can see or manipulate real hardware performance counters, a malicious hypervisor may exploit that channel.

docs.title: 3.2 Verification
docs.text: Inspect the launch configuration and the attested SEV_FEATURES claim. Confirm that bit 11 (VIRT_PERFMON) is not set. This is a launch feature, not the separate PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE guest-policy bit described in section 6. A guest-side check alone cannot prove that the launch setting was applied.

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text: Restricted injection limits the hypervisor to special #HV events instead of arbitrary interrupt injection.

docs.title: 4.2 Guest side requirements
docs.text:
For the guest to work safely with this feature:

  • guest firmware must support #HV handling
  • guest kernel must support #HV doorbell handling
  • host must provide the matching support

Do not enable or rely on restricted injection unless you have verified the full stack is ready.

Restricted injection is configured by the launch stack, not enabled by the guest commands in this guide. Follow the applicable AMD SEV-SNP documentation, Linux KVM AMD memory-encryption documentation, and QEMU AMD SEV documentation, along with the guest-firmware release documentation for the exact versions in use. Confirm that the complete host-kernel, QEMU, firmware, and guest-kernel stack supports the ABI-defined feature before enabling it; support may depend on vendor or downstream patches.

docs.title: 5.1 Check the report and enforce policy
docs.text:
Use Inspector to validate the report and enforce the required claims in Rego. In particular:

  • require ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE to be true
  • require PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE in the attested guest policy when required
  • compare every required guest-policy field with the approved deployment values (guest-policy correctness)
  • require prohibited launch features, such as VIRT_PERFMON, to be absent

Example attestation snippet

Platform Info (39):
  SMT Enabled: true
  TSME Enabled: true
  ECC Enabled: true
  RAPL Disabled: false
  Ciphertext Hiding Enabled: false
  Alias Check Complete: true

Illustrative rules to add to the existing Inspector policy. These assume that input.claims.attestations["snp"] contains the corresponding normalized claims; adjust field names to the Inspector claims available in the deployment. They add failures to the shared errors set, which the core policy uses to decide allow.

errors contains "SNP alias check is incomplete" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not snp.platform_info.alias_check_complete
}

errors contains "SNP page-swap restriction is not enabled" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not snp.guest_policy.page_swap_disable
}

errors contains "SNP guest policy does not match an approved policy" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not is_approved_snp_guest_policy(snp.guest_policy)
}

is_approved_snp_guest_policy(value) if {
    value in ref_values_by_type("SNP_GUEST_POLICY")
}

errors contains "SNP virtualized performance monitoring is enabled" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    snp.sev_features.virt_perfmon
}

Configure SNP_GUEST_POLICY reference values as the complete approved policy objects, guest policy is described in section 6. Include only the checks required for the deployment.

docs.title: 6. Harden SEV-SNP launch identity and policy
docs.text: The guest owner or launch service for example Tower selects several security-relevant values at launch. Review these values as part of image release and guest provisioning; they cannot generally be changed after launch.

docs.title: 6.1 Guest policy
docs.text:
Set the required guest policy through Tower. Select only the policy options required by the workload and platform. Review, where supported:

  • whether guest debugging is allowed (disable it for production)
  • whether SMT is allowed
  • whether a migration agent is allowed
  • whether the guest is restricted to a single socket
  • the minimum required ABI version
  • whether ciphertext hiding is required
  • whether RAPL must be disabled
  • whether AES-256-XTS is required
  • whether CXL devices are allowed

For deployments requiring page-swap restriction:

  • set PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE in the guest policy

PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE is bit 25 in the guest policy. It disables page swapping as defined by the applicable SNP ABI; it is not a general-purpose statement that all page movement is blocked. A verifier checks the attested guest-policy bit against the deployment's required value.

Illustrative rule to add to the existing Inspector policy. Map the field name to the normalized claim provided by Inspector:

errors contains "SNP page-swap restriction is not enabled" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not snp.guest_policy.page_swap_disable
}

To calculate the hardened policy value manually:

policy=$((0x30000 | (1 << 25)))
echo "policy = 0x$(printf '%x' $policy)"

Expected result:

0x20030000

In Tower if you select the desired policies, the policy values will be automatically created.

The exact available flags depend on the SEV-SNP ABI, platform generation, and launch tooling. Check the tool's documentation and confirm the resulting policy in the attestation report; do not assume that a requested option was applied.

docs.title: 6.2 Guest SVN and image identity
docs.text:
GUEST_SVN, FAMILY_ID, and IMAGE_ID are launch-time values supplied by the guest owner through the launch stack (for example, an ID block passed by the VMM). They are not normally chosen from inside the running guest. Whether Tower or another launcher sets them must be confirmed in that environment. In our current workflow, we do not set these values, so do not assume they identify an approved image until their values are observed in a real attestation report.

  • Guest SVN: owner-assigned version claim for the guest image. To enforce anti-rollback, the verifier must maintain a minimum acceptable SVN and reject reports below it. The field by itself does not make a verifier reject an older image.
  • Family ID and Image ID: owner-assigned identity labels that can help a verifier select or identify an image family/release when the launch stack populates and authenticates them.

These are separate report claims from MEASUREMENT. The measurement is the cryptographic digest of the guest launch contents; checking an Image ID does not avoid measurement verification and is not a substitute for it. An Image ID is useful as an additional, compact policy claim only when its source and binding are trusted. If these fields are used, record the expected claim values in the verifier policy and check them during attestation.

Illustrative rules to add to the existing Inspector policy. Configure the corresponding reference values for the deployment; store the minimum SVN reference value as a number:

is_approved_guest_svn(value) if {
    some minimum in ref_values_by_type("SNP_MIN_GUEST_SVN")
    value >= minimum
}

is_approved_snp_image_id(value) if {
    value in ref_values_by_type("SNP_IMAGE_ID")
}

errors contains "SNP guest SVN is below the approved minimum" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not is_approved_guest_svn(snp.guest_svn)
}

errors contains "SNP image ID is not approved" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not is_approved_snp_image_id(snp.image_id)
}

Apply the IMAGE_ID comparison only where the launch stack populates and authenticates that claim.

docs.title: 7. Bind runtime attestation to the Inspector challenge
docs.text:
For Inspector requests, Inspector generates a fresh nonce for each request and checks that the returned report's REPORT_DATA contains that request's expected nonce. This binds the report to the current challenge and helps prevent replay or substitution; it does not itself establish that the guest policy is secure. Verify the security claims separately by checking the attested guest policy and required report fields against the relying party's approved policy, as in section 5.

The report requester selects the VMPL in the report request. VMPL 0 is the highest privilege level; request the level appropriate to the component making the request, and have the verifier check the reported VMPL matches the intended component and trust policy.

docs.title: 8. Validate launch-time and current mitigation vectors
docs.text:
For attestation report versions that provide these fields (including supported report version 5 and later), inspect both vectors and interpret them using the matching AMD ABI/report-version definition:

  • LAUNCH_MIT_VECTOR: mitigation state recorded for guest launch.
  • CURRENT_MIT_VECTOR: mitigation state recorded when the attestation report is generated.

The vectors are bitmaps, not universal version numbers. Their numeric values and bit meanings depend on the report version and platform support, so there is no single expected hex value that applies to every SNP environment. For example, if policy requires mitigation M at launch and at report time, the policy should require the ABI-defined M bit to indicate the required state in both fields. If launch and current state differ, evaluate each field according to its own requirement; do not treat one as a replacement for the other.

docs.title: 8.1 Generate verifier policy for the deployment environment
docs.text:
Generate or configure the attestation policy from the actual environment rather than copying one policy across all platforms. Account for:

  • processor/platform generation and supported SNP report versions
  • firmware/ABI version and which claims the attestation pipeline exposes
  • expected Guest Policy, measurement, and any populated GUEST_SVN, FAMILY_ID, and IMAGE_ID claims
  • mitigation-vector bit meanings and required launch-time versus current states

The policy should check the claims required for that environment, reject missing claims when they are mandatory, and compare identity/SVN values against the approved image policy. Keep measurement verification enabled; identity labels are additional policy inputs, not a shortcut around it. Validate the policy against real reports from each supported environment before relying on it in production.

Illustrative rules to add to the existing Inspector policy. The example assumes Inspector (or an upstream normalization step) has mapped the ABI-defined bits to booleans; use the actual field names exposed by the deployment:

errors contains "required SNP launch mitigation is not enabled" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not snp.mitigations.launch_required
}

errors contains "required current SNP mitigation is not enabled" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not snp.mitigations.current_required
}

is_approved_snp_measurement(value) if {
    value in ref_values_by_type("SNP_MEASUREMENT")
}

errors contains "SNP measurement is not approved" if {
    snp := input.claims.attestations["snp"]
    not is_approved_snp_measurement(snp.measurement)
}

The mitigation fields above are illustrative normalized claims, not universal bit numbers. Obtain the actual vector values from the target launch stack and map them using the matching AMD ABI. Add identity checks only for claims populated and authenticated in the environment.

docs.title: 9. Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Guest firmware is SNP-aware and the guest kernel is current, with SNP support and #HV handling where required
  • [ ] VIRT_PERFMON (SEV_FEATURES[11]) is not enabled for PMC virtualization
  • [ ] PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE is enabled in the launch policy when supported and required
  • [ ] Restricted Injection is used only when the host kernel, QEMU, guest firmware, and guest kernel all support it
  • [ ] Guest Policy is reviewed and set by the authorized guest owner or Tower
  • [ ] Debugging is disabled in production unless explicitly approved
  • [ ] Guest SVN meets the anti-rollback policy; Family ID and Image ID match the approved image
  • [ ] Verifier policy is generated for the platform/report environment and checks required identity, SVN, policy, and mitigation claims
  • [ ] Attestation report confirms the expected guest policy and required claims
  • [ ] ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE is true in the attestation report
  • [ ] REPORT_DATA is bound to a fresh Inspector nonce and validated by Inspector
  • [ ] The report is requested at the intended VMPL
  • [ ] LAUNCH_MIT_VECTOR and CURRENT_MIT_VECTOR are interpreted using the matching AMD ABI and checked against environment-specific requirements

docs.title: AMD SEV-SNP - Host Hardening
docs.text: This guide covers the host-side hardening controls for AMD SEV-SNP environments. It focuses on firmware, kernel, hypervisor, launch-time policy, and attestation checks that a host owner must validate before production deployment.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
The host must ensure that confidential guests are launched with the correct protections and that the virtualization stack does not enable unsafe features.

Key host-side objectives:

  • keep firmware and host software updated
  • verify the kernel supports SEV-SNP
  • verify QEMU/KVM supports the required guest launch features
  • ensure guest policy disables unsafe features
  • validate attestation results

docs.title: 2.1 Confirm CPU and platform capabilities
docs.text:
Check platform logs:

dmesg | grep -Ei 'sev|snp|kvm'
journalctl -k | grep -Ei 'sev|snp|kvm'

Check Current SEV-SNP Status:

# Quick capability check
sudo dmesg | grep -E 'SEV|SNP|RMP'

# Using sevctl / snphost (recommended)
# Install from https://github.com/virtee/snphost
sevctl ok snp
# or
snphost ok
Expected output should confirm SEV-SNP and RMP table initialization.

docs.title: 3.1 Firmware
docs.text:
Update the platform BIOS/UEFI and AMD PSP/SEV-SNP firmware: Download the latest firmware matching the CPU family from the AMD developer site (https://www.amd.com/en/developer/sev.html).

Use these commands on the host to find CPU family:

lscpu
cat /proc/cpuinfo
More specifically: 

lscpu | egrep 'Architecture|Vendor ID|Model name|CPU family|Model|Stepping'

After finding the CPU family download the new firmware. Example for EPYC 7003 (Milan / Fam 19h Model 0xh):

wget https://download.amd.com/developer/eula/sev/amd_sev_fam19h_model0xh_1.58.02.zip
unzip amd_sev_fam19h_model0xh_1.58.02.zip

Install fimware:

sudo mkdir -p /lib/firmware/amd
sudo cp amd_sev_fam19h_model0xh_1.58.02.sbin /lib/firmware/amd/amd_sev_fam19h_model0xh.sbin
Reload the CCP/SEV driver (or reboot):

sudo rmmod kvm_amd
sudo rmmod ccp
sudo modprobe ccp
sudo modprobe kvm_amd
Verfy:

sudo dmesg | grep -E 'SEV-SNP|firmware|PSP'
snphost show

Example output after a successful update:

[   ] SEV-SNP: RMP table physical range [0x0000000093300000 - 0x00000000a38fffff]
[   ] AMD-Vi: IOMMU SNP support enabled.
[   ] AMD-Vi: Extended features (0x841f77e022094ace, 0x0): PPR X2APIC NX IA GA PC SNP
[   ] ccp 0000:45:00.1: SEV firmware updated from 1.55.31 to 1.58.2
[   ] ccp 0000:45:00.1: SEV-SNP API:1.58 build:2
[   ] ccp 0000:45:00.1: SEV API:1.58 build:2
[   ] kvm_amd: SEV enabled (ASIDs 100 - 509)
[   ] kvm_amd: SEV-ES enabled (ASIDs 1 - 99)
[   ] kvm_amd: SEV-SNP enabled (ASIDs 1 - 99)

docs.title: 3.2 Host Kernel Upgrade
docs.text:
Use the distro or vendor update flow:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
# or
sudo dnf upgrade -y
# or
sudo zypper update

Check the active kernel:

uname -r

docs.title: 4. Restricted Injection (Ahoi / WeSee / Heckler mitigation)
docs.text:
Restricted injection limits the interrupts a VMM can inject into an SNP guest. It is intended to mitigate malicious-interrupt attacks such as WeSee and Heckler. Support and setup depend on the exact kernel, QEMU, OVMF, and guest-kernel versions; do not infer availability from a version number or from the presence of a source file alone.

The host needs a kernel with the Restricted Injection KVM/SVM support and #HV doorbell handling.

QEMU and SNP-aware OVMF must support the launch configuration for Restricted Injection. In the SNP firmware ABI, the corresponding launch feature is SEV_FEATURES[3].

Do not rely on older statements about whether support is mainline or exposed as a QEMU property; verify the current release notes and configuration interface for each deployed component.

The guest kernel must also support #HV doorbell handling.

Check whether the kernel includes the required support for SEV-SNP and restricted injection.

grep -RIn "restricted injection\|#HV doorbell\|doorbell page" /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build/arch/x86/kvm/svm 2>/dev/null

If you have a local kernel tree:

git -C /usr/src/linux log --grep='restricted injection' --grep='#HV'
git -C /usr/src/linux log --grep='doorbell'

The host must confirm all layers support restricted injection before enabling it in production.

Required support stack:

  • host kernel: yes
  • KVM/SVM support: yes
  • QEMU: yes
  • guest firmware: SNP-aware, supports #HV
  • guest kernel: guest-side #HV support, yes

If a layer is missing support, do not assume the guest receives the protection.

References:

  • AMD SEV-SNP Firmware ABI Specification (Publication 56860) — ABI definition of launch feature bits, including SEV_FEATURES[3].
  • Linux KVM AMD memory-encryption documentation and the Linux KVM/SVM SEV implementation — host-side SEV/KVM context. These do not by themselves establish that a particular kernel build includes Restricted Injection.

docs.title: 5. Checklist
docs.text:
Before deployment, confirm the following:

  • [ ] BIOS/UEFI and AMD PSP/firmware are updated
  • [ ] host kernel supports SEV-SNP and required KVM features
  • [ ] QEMU/KVM stack supports the guest launch configuration
  • [ ] restricted injection is enabled only where all layers support it
  • [ ] host launch settings match the approved guest policy and are confirmed by attestation policy

A hardened SEV-SNP host is not defined by one setting alone. It is a combination of:

  • updated firmware
  • modern kernel and hypervisor
  • correct launch-time feature selection
  • a verified guest policy

Guest-policy requirements, including PMC virtualization, PAGE_SWAP_DISABLE, and attestation checks such as ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE, are covered in the SNP guest hardening guide.

The host owner must verify actual platform state rather than assume default values are secure.

docs.title: Intel TDX Guest Hardening
docs.text: This guide covers the guest-side controls for Intel TDX confidential VMs. It explains the kernel parameters, filter settings, and attestation checks required for a hardened TD.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text: The TD should run with the smallest required device, I/O, and ACPI surface. It must avoid trusting host-controlled time and entropy sources and must be verifiable through attestation.

docs.title: 2. Required production kernel parameters
docs.text:
These are guest Linux kernel command-line parameters, not commands to run in a shell. Configure them in the guest image's bootloader (for example, its GRUB configuration) or have the VMM supply the guest command line at launch. The exact mechanism depends on the image and platform; coordinate with the host operator when the VMM controls the command line. After reboot, /proc/cmdline shows the parameters active in the running guest.

Use the hardened guest configuration:

mce=off
oops=panic
pci=noearly
pci=nommconf
no-kvmclock
random.trust_cpu=y

Apply them to the guest kernel command line and reboot.

cat /proc/cmdline

docs.title: 3. Keep the device filter enabled
docs.text: The TDX guest should use the default allow-list model. The guest kernel applies the filter; the image owner configures guest kernel parameters and the VMM may supply or override the boot command line. Coordinate both sides and verify the effective setting in the running guest.

docs.title: 3.1 Recommended practice
docs.text:
Only allow the minimal set of drivers required by the workload, such as:

  • virtio_net
  • virtio_console
  • virtio_blk
  • 9pnet_virtio

docs.title: 3.2 Do not disable the filter in production
docs.text:
tdx_disable_filter

tdx_disable_filter is a guest kernel command-line parameter, not a shell command. Do not include it in the guest bootloader configuration or allow the VMM to pass it at launch. Check /proc/cmdline in the running guest to confirm it is absent.

docs.title: 3.3 Extra device allowances
docs.text:
If needed, use explicit allow-list entries:

authorize_allow_devs=pci:<ven_id:dev_id>

Use this sparingly and only for approved devices.

docs.title: 4. Restrict Port I/O and PCI access
docs.text: The guest kernel enforces these restrictions; the host/VMM controls which virtual devices and launch parameters are presented. Keep the two configurations consistent and verify the effective guest policy after boot.

docs.title: 4.1 Port I/O
docs.text: Only a minimal set of I/O ports should be accessible. Do not expose extra ports unless absolutely required.

docs.title: 4.2 PCI config space
docs.text: The PCI restrictions listed in section 2 reduce unsafe probing and limit access to untrusted or unnecessary config space.

docs.title: 5. Restrict ACPI tables
docs.text:
Configure any guest kernel command-line options through the guest bootloader or the VMM-provided command line described in section 2.

Use the minimal accepted ACPI set rather than broad expansion.

Do not use broad table exceptions in production.

tdx_allow_acpi=

This should be used only for debug or tightly controlled exceptions.

docs.title: 6. Use secure randomness and secure time
6.1 Secure random source
docs.text: The random.trust_cpu=y parameter from section 2 selects the architectural DRNG and avoids weak entropy fallback.

docs.title: 6.2 Time source
docs.text: The no-kvmclock parameter from section 2 prevents reliance on the host-controlled KVM clock and leaves the TD using the platform's supported TSC time source.

docs.title: 7. Keep the runtime restricted and consistent
docs.text: These are guest-runtime requirements. The host/VMM must not configure guest launch or paravirtual interfaces in a way that contradicts the approved guest profile.

docs.title: 7.1 Use the default hardened interrupt model
docs.text: The guest should rely on virtualized x2APIC and the TDX module’s interrupt mediation. Legacy xAPIC MMIO and unsafe host-injected interrupt patterns are not appropriate for production TDs.

docs.title: 7.2 Use the minimal hypercall/PV set
docs.text: Only keep the required KVM or PV features; do not turn on unnecessary host-facing interfaces.

docs.title: 8. Validate runtime and attestation state
docs.text:
Check the running cmdline:

cat /proc/cmdline

Compare the active command line with the hardened parameters in section 2. Also validate attestation output for:

  • device filter is active
  • ACPI list is restricted
  • kernel cmdline matches the hardened profile
  • no broad or unsafe device exceptions are in effect

Inspector policy should validate only claims that its configured verifier actually exposes. Confirm the normalized claim names and enforcement behavior against the deployment's Inspector configuration; do not assume that every item in this list is checked automatically.

docs.title: 9. Mitigate StumbleStepping and other side channels
docs.text:
Updating the TDX Module does not eliminate every fine-grained side channel. Intel treats residual leakage such as StumbleStepping as a software mitigation concern, similar to other microarchitectural side channels.

The constant-time software guidance in this section also applies to SEV-SNP workloads; see the SNP guest hardening guide.

docs.title: 9.1 Keep cryptographic software current
docs.text:
Update the guest OS, cryptographic libraries, and applications using the distribution's supported update mechanism.

  • OpenSSL 3.3.1 or newer
  • wolfSSL 5.6.6 or newer

Check installed versions where applicable:

openssl version
pkg-config --modversion wolfssl 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: 9.2 Use constant-time cryptographic implementations
docs.text:
Treat the hypervisor as able to observe fine-grained memory-access patterns, potentially at cache-line granularity. For code that handles secrets:

  • avoid secret-dependent branches, memory addresses, and execution time
  • use vetted cryptographic libraries and APIs with documented constant-time behavior instead of writing cryptographic primitives
  • avoid early-exit comparisons for passwords, MACs, and padding; use constant-time comparison routines supplied by the library
  • use constant-time modular exponentiation and secret-independent table selection for RSA and Diffie-Hellman operations
  • avoid secret-indexed lookup tables, such as conventional AES S-box tables; use vetted constant-time implementations

Compiler transformations and CPU behavior can invalidate home-grown constant-time techniques. Review the generated implementation and use security-reviewed libraries rather than assuming that a source-level construct such as a conditional move guarantees constant-time execution.

Follow Intel's current Trust Domain Security Guidance for Developers and the applicable software side-channel guidance.

Note: For now in cbclient we use RSA rust crypto library which is non-constant crypto algorithm and we should look for future patches that fix this issue.

docs.title: 10. Verify Intel TDX TCB recovery status
docs.text:
TDX security depends on a Trusted Computing Base (TCB), including platform firmware, microcode, the TDX Module, and related components. After Intel releases a security fix, the affected component's Security Version Number (SVN) and Intel's attestation collateral may be updated through a TCB Recovery (TCB-R).

Installing an update is necessary but does not by itself prove to a relying party that the platform is at an acceptable TCB level. The quote must be checked against current Intel Provisioning Certification Service (PCS) collateral and an explicit trust policy.

docs.title: 10.1 Guest or workload owner actions
docs.text:
Before releasing secrets or trusting a TD:

  1. Request a fresh quote from the TD using the deployment's attestation workflow.
  2. Verify the quote and its TCB status against current Intel PCS collateral using an approved verifier, such as Inspector, Intel DCAP, Intel Trust Authority, or Confidential Containers Trustee.
  3. Enforce a documented policy over the verified result: require the latest TCB, allow a defined grace period, or pin an approved intermediate TCB evaluation data number. Do not infer acceptance merely from successful quote verification.
  4. Decide whether a TD created before a platform update may continue running, or must be restarted so it is created under the updated TCB.

Note: in our platform the verification is done by Inspector.

The guest cannot change platform TCB values such as CPUSVN or TEE_TCB_SVN. A guest can choose to restart itself, but only the platform and TDX Module determine the platform TCB reflected by attestation.

Illustrative rules to add to the existing Inspector policy. These assume Inspector exposes the verified TDX status under input.claims.attestations["tdx"].tcb_status; adjust the path to the normalized claims in your deployment and configure accepted statuses as reference values.

is_accepted_tdx_tcb_status(value) if {
    value in ref_values_by_type("TDX_ACCEPTED_TCB_STATUS")
}

errors contains "TDX TCB status is not accepted" if {
    tdx := input.claims.attestations["tdx"]
    not is_accepted_tdx_tcb_status(tdx.tcb_status)
}

The accepted status set should reflect the organization's choice between strict latest-TCB enforcement and an explicitly bounded grace period. Inspector's quote signature verification, collateral, and freshness validation must also succeed; this policy check selects which verified TCB statuses the relying party accepts.

docs.title: 10.2 PCS collateral selection
docs.text:
Intel PCS supports collateral selection parameters for TCB information. Inspector should retrieve the collateral needed to evaluate both the strict/latest and grace-period views where supported, then expose the verified result for the Rego policy to accept or reject. The exact TDX certification API and FMSPC come from the platform's quote/collateral:

  • update=early: request the latest available TCB information; use for strict, prompt enforcement of TCB-R updates.
  • update=standard: request the standard collateral level, which may include a grace period. Do not assume it means the latest TCB.
  • tcbEvaluationDataNumber=<number>: request a specific evaluation data number when supported by the API. It cannot be combined with update.

The following illustrates the Intel PCS update=early query form from the SGX certification API; a TDX verifier must use the corresponding TDX certification endpoint:

https://api.trustedservices.intel.com/sgx/certification/v4/tcb?fmspc=<FMSPC>&update=early

Do not treat a collateral response or URL alone as quote verification. Use a maintained verifier that validates the quote chain, signatures, TCB status, and current collateral. If Inspector fetches more than one collateral view, the policy must explicitly identify which verified status values it accepts.

Deployment action: configure Inspector to retrieve the collateral views needed for the selected policy (including both early and standard where supported) and expose their verified TCB results to Rego. Do not silently rely on the PCS default of standard when the policy requires strict latest-TCB enforcement.

docs.title: 10.3 Platform owner and organization actions
docs.text:
• monitor Intel Platform Updates and TCB Recovery Attestation information for affected processors and required actions
  • deploy applicable BIOS, microcode, TDX Module, and other platform updates
  • re-register updated platforms with Intel where required so current PCK certificates and collateral can be issued
  • support runtime updates where the platform supports them; otherwise plan a warm or cold reset as required
  • publish the current TCB level, update cadence, and any grace-period policy to tenants
  • configure verification services to use current collateral and enforce the organization's policy
  • for migratable TDs, include the Migration TD and destination platform in the trust review and attestation policy

docs.title: 11. Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Guest kernel includes TDX support and is kept current
  • [ ] Production kernel arguments from section 2 are active
  • [ ] Device filter is enabled and only required devices are allowed
  • [ ] tdx_disable_filter is absent; device exceptions are explicit and reviewed
  • [ ] Port I/O and PCI access are restricted
  • [ ] ACPI table allow-list is minimal; broad tdx_allow_acpi exceptions are absent
  • [ ] Runtime uses the intended x2APIC and minimal hypercall/PV configuration
  • [ ] OpenSSL is at least 3.3.1 or wolfSSL is at least 5.6.6 where used, with current vendor security updates applied
  • [ ] Secret-handling code uses vetted constant-time cryptographic operations and avoids secret-dependent branches, addresses, and early-exit comparisons
  • [ ] A fresh quote is obtained and verified with current Intel PCS collateral before secrets are released
  • [ ] TCB trust policy is explicit (early, standard, or an approved evaluation data number)
  • [ ] Platform updates, required resets, and any TD restart policy are addressed
  • [ ] Migration and destination-platform verification are included when TD migration is used

docs.title: Intel TDX Host Hardening
docs.text: This guide covers the host-side environment for Intel TDX deployments. It focuses on the host requirements needed to launch and manage hardened TD guests safely.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
The host should provide a trusted execution environment for TDX guests and ensure the guest launch configuration does not relax the security model.

Key host-side duties:

  • keep platform firmware and TDX module updated
  • keep kernel up to date
  • verify host and hypervisor support for trusted guest deployment
  • ensure guest launches use a hardened configuration
  • confirm attestation data reflects the expected runtime policy

docs.title: 2.1 Confirm platform support
docs.text:
uname -a
lscpu
grep -Ei 'tdx|vmx' /proc/cpuinfo

Check kernel messages and logs:

dmesg | grep -Ei 'tdx|kvm'
journalctl -k | grep -Ei 'tdx|kvm'
Make sure there is no error in logs.

docs.title: 3. Keep firmware and host kernel updated
3.1 Platform firmware
docs.text:
Update BIOS/UEFI and Intel TDX-related firmware or module versions as follows.

Update Intel TDX Module via BIOS update

Steps:

  • Reach out to your OEM/ODM or Independent BIOS Vendor (IBV) to ask for a BIOS containing another version of the Intel TDX Module.
  • Once available, retrieve the BIOS update.
  • Flash BIOS update according the instructions of the BIOS provider.

Update Intel TDX Module via Binary Deployment

Steps:

  • Download the Intel TDX Module binary:

To download a specific version of an Intel TDX Module and a corresponding signature structure, navigate to the releases page of the Intel TDX Module. Download the archive intel_tdx_module.tar.gz from the release you want to use.

  • Unpack the downloaded archive:
tar -xvzf intel_tdx_module.tar.gz

If not done before, create an EFI directory: 

sudo mkdir -p /boot/efi/EFI/TDX/

  • Copy the Intel TDX Module binary and the corresponding signature structure to the EFI directly created in step 3. 
    sudo cp TDX-Module/intel_tdx_module.so \
    /boot/efi/EFI/TDX/TDX-SEAM.so
sudo cp TDX-Module/intel_tdx_module.so.sigstruct \
    /boot/efi/EFI/TDX/TDX-SEAM.so.sigstruct
  • Check that the copied files are present in /boot/efi/EFI/TDX/ with a current date: 
    sudo ls -ls /boot/efi/EFI/TDX/
  • Reboot the host.

References:

  • Intel TDX Enabling Guide — Update TDX module.
  • Intel TDX Module releases — release binaries, signature structures, hashes, and release-specific instructions. Verify downloaded artifacts against the published release information and follow the instructions for the target platform.
  • For BIOS/UEFI updates, follow the instructions and compatibility guidance published by the system OEM/ODM or IBV.

docs.title: 3.2 Host virtualization stack
docs.text:
Update the host kernel and KVM/QEMU stack to the latest supported versions for TDX guest launch and secure runtime behavior.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
# or
sudo dnf upgrade -y
# or
sudo zypper update

docs.title: 4. Make sure the host launches guests with hardened defaults
docs.text:
The host/VMM supplies the guest command line when it owns guest boot configuration. Apply the kernel parameters listed in the TDX guest guide through the platform's supported launch configuration. If the guest image manages its own bootloader, coordinate with its owner and verify that the resulting launch matches the approved profile.

These guest parameters and their in-guest verification are maintained in the guest guide to avoid conflicting copies.

docs.title: 5. Keep the device and I/O surface minimal
docs.text: The host should not launch guests that disable TDX device filtering or admit broad untrusted device access.

docs.title: 5.1 Avoid unsafe guest launch patterns
docs.text:
Do not pass this guest kernel command-line parameter in production; it disables the device filter:

tdx_disable_filter

Avoid broad ACPI or device exceptions unless justified and fully reviewed.

docs.title: 5.2 Recommended controls
docs.text:
• keep the device allow-list minimal
  • restrict port I/O access
  • limit ACPI table acceptance
  • avoid unrestricted device expansion

In summary do not use in production:

tdx_disable_filter
unrestricted tdx_allow_acpi=
unrestricted authorize_allow_devs=

These options are measured into the attestation quote (RTMRs / cmdline).

docs.title: 6. Ensure only trusted guest configuration is accepted
docs.text:
The host should reject or at least flag launch profiles with:

  • broad ACPI permitting
  • unrestricted device allow-lists
  • disabled filtering
  • legacy timer behavior
  • weak entropy configuration

docs.title: 7. Verify launch configuration and guest attestation
docs.text:
Before production, confirm that the VMM launch configuration supplies the approved guest profile and that attestation verifies the required runtime claims. The guest owner checks its active /proc/cmdline as described in the guest guide; the host owner checks the launch configuration and the verified quote/claims.

  • filter state
  • allowed device set
  • ACPI restrictions
  • any launch-measured command-line or runtime claims required by policy

docs.title: 8. Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] host firmware updated
  • [ ] host kernel and KVM/QEMU stack updated
  • [ ] guest launch config follows hardened profile
  • [ ] device filter remains enabled
  • [ ] no broad ACPI or device exceptions enabled
  • [ ] no-kvmclock enforced
  • [ ] random.trust_cpu=y enforced
  • [ ] guest attestation validates runtime security posture

A secure Intel TDX host environment depends on controlled guest launch policy and runtime verification. The host must not assume that a running TD is secure simply because it boots; attestation and runtime policy checks are required.

docs.title: CanaryBit Inspector
docs.text:
Audit & Certify Trusted Execution Environments (TEE)

CanaryBit Inspector is a Confidential Computing Remote Attestation service with extended functionality. It lets you fully verify the security of your processing environments before any sensitive data analysis. Inspector confirms that the underlying platform supports and actually uses the Confidential Computing capabilities of its processor architecture and firmware. It does this by validating an attestation report collected by a lightweight client running inside the TEE, which gathers information at the hardware, virtualization, OS and software levels. Inspector then monitors infrastructure security and enforces your deployment policies by alerting components that fail to meet them.

Key capabilities

  • Confidential VM and container attestation: verify Confidential VMs deployed through CanaryBit Tower, through your own cloud-init configuration, or manually. Confidential containers and pods are attested with CanaryBit Surveyor, whether they run on a managed service such as AKS or EKS or on another container platform.
  • Broad hardware coverage: supports AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX, and exposes NVIDIA Attestation Services for GPU attestation (subject to the NVIDIA End-user License Agreement).
  • Custom policies: enforce your own Rego policies at the application, operating system, virtualization and hardware levels, on top of the verifier's default policies. The dashboard's Policy Generator and Policy Playground help you write them.
  • Unified dashboard: fine-tune expected environments, review vulnerabilities (CVEs) affecting your setup, and download verification reports and insights.
  • Flexible licensing: Trial (free, Not For Resale), Private (Basic, Standard or Enterprise), and Reseller for offering Inspector as a service. It can be deployed on-prem, for internal use, or offered as a service.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
CanaryBit Inspector service is built on microservices that wholetogether provide an holistic view on the underlying insfrastructure and technology stack.

  • Core: the core logic of CanaryBit's Inspector Remote Attestations (RA) service. It verifies the integrity of a processing environment running on hardware with Confidential Computing capabilities. https://api.inspector.confidentialcloud.io

  • Dashboard: it offers multiple services and functionalities to fine-tune the expected processing environments and collect the final results through a single, unified interface. https://dashboard.inspector.confidentialcloud.io

  • Vulnerabilities Search: it structures and exposes CVE vulnerabilities to the Inspector dashboard, highlighting security vulnerabilities of the target setup.

  • Cache: it optimises the retrieval of hardware certificates (leaf, intermediate and root) and relevant assets needed for cryptographic verification of the attestation reports generated by Confidential Computing-capable processing units.

  • Database: a data store used by all the microservices;

docs.title: The client
docs.text: The cb-inspector-client is the client implementation for the CanaryBit Inspector Attestation service. Written in Rust, it is responsible to collect the attestation data and call the CanaryBit Inspector API to verify the execution environments, either Confidential VMs or containers.

docs.title: Attest a Confidential VM
docs.text: CanaryBit Inspector verifies Confidential VMs (cVM) deployed:

docs.title: CanaryBit Tower
docs.text: A Confidential VM is automatically deployed by the end-user using CanaryBit Tower on the target infrastructure provider and attested by CanaryBit Inspector via the CanaryBit cloud-init configuration injected at creation time.

docs.text: A Confidential VM is deployed by the end-user on the target infrastructure provider and attested by CanaryBit Inspector via a custom cloud-init configuration injected at creation time containing the steps required by CanaryBit Inspector.

docs.title: Manually
docs.text:
A Confidential VM is deployed by the end-user on the target infrastructure provider and manually attested by CanaryBit Inspector following the steps below:

From outside a Confidential VM:

  1. Download the CanaryBit Command-Line Interface (CLI)

  2. Source your CanaryBit credentials:

    export CB_USERNAME=***
export CB_PASSWORD=***

  3. Download the CanaryBit Inspector client (cb-inspector-client)

    ./cb download cb-inspector-client

  4. Get a Token

    ./cb login inspector

    The command returns a fresh token for the user. The token will be used by cb-inspector-client to authenticate the user towards the CanaryBit Inspector service.

From inside a Confidential VM:

  1. Access the Confidential VM and run the cb-inspector-client using the fresh token retrieved in the previous step:
export CB_INSPECTOR_CLIENT_TOKEN=***

./cb-inspector-client --environments [TARGET_ENV] --inspector-url https://api.inspector.confidentialcloud.io

where TARGET_ENV is currently, one of the following:

  • snp for AMD SEV-SNP
  • tdx for Intel TDX

Note

Currently, cb-inspector-client requires the libtss2 library to be installed on the machine. If not available, simply install the package with: 

sudo apt install libtss2-dev

Example: AMD SEV-SNP attestation

docs.text:
In addition to Confidential VMs, CanaryBit Inspector can attest confidential containers/pods, no matter if they are managed by an orchestration service (e.g. Azure AKS or AWS EKS) or a specific container platform.

docs.title: Add custom policies
docs.text:
CanaryBit Inspector allows end-users to apply custom policies at different levels in the technology stack:

  • Application
  • Operating System
  • Virtualization
  • Hardware

Custom policies are enforced in addition to the verifier policies, and together they assess the security level and prove the correctness of each TEE.

The Policy Generator and Policy Playground in the CanaryBit Inspector dashboard help you define custom policies according to the exposed CanaryBit Inspector report object schema.

docs.title: Create a policy file
docs.text:
Create a file with a custom Rego policy expression.

Example

Custom policy to enforce a specific OS kernel version, hypervisor, and region for the deployed TEE.

mypolicy.rego
package mypolicy

default allow := false

allow if {
    input.claims.attestations.canarybit.kernel_version == "6.17.0-14-generic"
    input.claims.metadata.hypervisor.cpuid_hypervisor == "HyperV"
    input.claims.metadata.instance.region = "northeurope"
}

docs.text:

For manual verification, simply add the policy file as argument to the cb-inspector-client.

Example: Manual verification with custom policy

./cb-inspector-client ... --policy mypolicy.rego

docs.title: CanaryBit Surveyor
docs.text:
Safeguard Container execution

CanaryBit Surveyor is a confidential container launcher that runs containers and pods only after the underlying infrastructure has been validated. It works with Kata Containers or directly on confidential nodes in your Kubernetes cluster running on AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX hardware. Each workload is remotely attested by CanaryBit Inspector before it starts and then re-verified on a schedule (daily by default), so your data and algorithms stay protected inside a hardware-encrypted execution environment.

Key capabilities

  • Attestation-gated deployment: workloads launch only after the infrastructure passes remote attestation.
  • Two deployment modes: kata (recommended) isolates each pod in its own lightweight VM. node runs pods directly on confidential nodes, which gives security but no isolation between pods.
  • Custom policies: add your own Rego policies, for example to enforce a kernel version, hypervisor or region, on top of the default verifier policies. Verification reports: download attestation reports and insights from the Inspector dashboard.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A CanaryBit account;
  • A CanaryBit Inspector licence;
  • The CanaryBit CLI (cb-cli) installed;
  • Access to a Kubernetes cluster (kubeconfig) running on a supported hardware platform;
  • Only for kata mode:
    • Helm installed.

docs.title: Source your credentials
docs.text:
Source your CanaryBit credentials (e.g. cb.rc):

cb.rc
export CB_USERNAME=***
export CB_PASSWORD=***

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
There are two ways to download CanaryBit Surveyor:

  1. Through the CanaryBit Inspector dashboard

  2. Via the CanaryBit CLI.

    # View all available versions
$ cb list surveyor

# Install the latest version for your platform
$ cb download surveyor

# Check all possible values for platform
$ cb download --help

# Install the latest version for a specific platform
$ cb download surveyor --target <platform>

Example

$ cb list surveyor
0.2.0
0.3.0

$ cb download surveyor --target macos-arm64
Downloaded surveyor-macos-arm64 to surveyor-macos-arm64-0.3.0

docs.title: Install Kata (recommended)
docs.text:
Only for kata mode, hardware-specific Kata Containers runtime classes are required before deploying confidential workloads.

To install the Kata runtime classes, first initialize the configuration with: 

$ surveyor kata init

Info

CanaryBit Surveyor uses node-feature-discovery labels to identify the cluster nodes with Confidential Computing capabilities:

labels = [
  "feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-security.sev.snp.enabled",
  "feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-security.tdx.enabled",
]

Then, install the hardware-specific kata runtime classes (kata-qemu-snp and kata-qemu-tdx) with:

$ surveyor kata setup

docs.title: Initialize Surveyor
docs.text:
Configure CanaryBit Surveyor to use the right CanaryBit Inspector and registry endpoint:

$ surveyor init

docs.title: Create new secrets
docs.text:
Surveyor requires two secrets to perform a remote attestation:

  • the inspector secret to authenticate to CanaryBit Inspector and refresh the user's access token overtime;
  • the registry secret to pull the CanaryBit Inspector client (cb-inspector-client) container image.

To create new secrets, first login via the CanaryBit CLI and export your authentication token (CB_TOKENS):

$ export CB_TOKENS=$(cb login)

Then, create both inspector and registry secret on your cluster with :

$ surveyor secret create canarybit --namespace default

docs.title: Add custom policies
docs.text:
It's possible to add a custom policies (e.g. mypolicy.rego) at different levels in the technology stack (hardware, hypervisor, OS and more). Custom policies will be enforced on top of the verifier defaults policies, and together assess both the security level and correctness of each TEE.

To create a custom policy, simply create a file with a custom Rego policy expression.

Example

A custom policy to enforce a specific OS kernel version, hypervisor, and region for the deployed TEE.

mypolicy.rego
package mypolicy

default allow := false

allow if {
  input.claims.attestations.canarybit.kernel_version == "6.17.0-14-generic"
  input.claims.metadata.hypervisor.cpuid_hypervisor == "HyperV"
  input.claims.metadata.instance.region = "northeurope"
}

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Deploy your container (e.g. mypod.yaml) via Pod/Deployment manifest:

$ surveyor deploy --cc-mode kata --kata-runtime-class kata-qemu-snp --attestation-targets snp --attestation-policy mypolicy.rego mypod.yaml

How it works

CanaryBit Surveyor will extend the Pod manifest by adding the CanaryBit Inspector client (cb-inspector-client) as init container, ensuring the workload is launched only upon a successful attestation and verified by CanaryBit Inspector at a custom schedule (defaults to daily)

Pod Logs

Pod Logs are enabled or disabled depending on the selected containerization platform and its confidential kata-runtime implementation. For example, RedHat Openshift kata-cc runtime disables pod logs by default (ReadStreamRequest:=false), whereas upstream kata-qemu-snp and kata-qemu-tdx leaves stdout enabled (ReadStreamRequest:=true) by default unless explicitly enforced via a policy with pod annotation.

docs.text:
Orchestrate Trusted Execution Environments (TEE)

CanaryBit Tower is a Confidential Computing resource orchestration service that helps you deploy secure processing environments and control configuration drift. Delivered as Infrastructure as Code (IaC) configurations, it creates the required infrastructure resources and one or more TEEs, either on the cloud provider of your choice or on-premises.

Key capabilities

  • Infrastructure as code: provision Confidential VMs and their supporting resources (networks, security groups and more) with a standard init and apply workflow.
  • Multi-environment support: free, Apache-2.0 licensed configurations for Azure, AWS and GCP. VMware, Proxmox, OpenShift and Libvirt/QEMU for bare-metal and private setups require a Premium License.
  • Remote attestation: verify each Confidential VM's security characteristics at boot time or at a custom cadence with CanaryBit Inspector, so you aren't left trusting the hypervisor or infrastructure provider.
  • Custom policies: add your own Rego policies at different levels of the stack (hardware, hypervisor, OS and more), enforced on top of the verifier's default policies.
  • Verification reports: download the final report and additional insights from the Inspector dashboard.

The host BIOS must support the features and be configured correctly before the kernel or hypervisor can use them. Menu names, exact option labels, and even the presence of some settings vary by OEM (Dell, Lenovo, HPE, Supermicro, etc.) and by BIOS version.

Warning

Always check with OEM/ODM or independent BIOS vendor for the precise path and recommended values on the platform. The examples below are common patterns only.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Socket Configuration → Processor Configuration

    Memory Encryption (TME)                             → Enabled
    Total Memory Encryption (TME) Bypass                → Disabled
    Total Memory Encryption Multi-Tenant (TME-MT)       → Enabled
    Memory Integrity                                    → Enabled 
    Trust Domain Extension (TDX)                        → Enabled
    TDX Secure Arbitration Mode Loader (SEAM Loader)    → Enabled 
    TME-MT / TDX key split                              → 1
    SW Guard Extensions (SGX)                           → Enabled
    SGX PRM / PRMRR size                                → 2 GB (or more)

More information on the Intel official host setup documentation.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Log into the host and run:

sudo dmesg | grep -i tdx

Expect a line such as virt/tdx: module initialized, preceded by virt/tdx: BIOS enabled: private KeyID range.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Advanced → AMD CBS → CPU Common Options

    SMEE                              → Enabled
    SEV Control                       → Enabled
    SEV-ES ASID Space Limit           → 100
    SNP Memory (RMP Table) Coverage   → Enabled

Advanced → NBIO Common Options → IOMMU/Security

    SEV-SNP Support                   → Enabled
    IOMMU                             → Enabled

More information on the AMD official host setup documentation.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Log into the host and run:

sudo dmesg | grep -i -e rmp -e sev
cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/sev_snp

Expect SEV-SNP: RMP table physical range ..., kvm_amd: SEV-SNP enabled (ASIDs 1 - N), and Y from the sysfs file.

docs.title: CanaryBit Command-Line Interface (CLI)
docs.text:
Manage CanaryBit resources with interactive commands

The CanaryBit Command-Line Interface (CLI) is a cross-platform command-line tool to connect to your CanaryBit account and execute commands on CanaryBit resources.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • A CanaryBit account;

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
List all available versions:

$ curl -s "https://canarybit-public-binaries.s3.amazonaws.com/?prefix=cb-cli/" | grep -oE '<Key>[^<]+</Key>' | sed -E 's/<\/?Key>//g' | awk -F'/' 'NF>2 {print $2}' | sort -u | awk '{printf "  📁  %s\n", $0}'

Download the binary from CanaryBit's S3 public bucket:

$ curl -fsSL https://canarybit-public-binaries.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/cb-cli/[VERSION]/[OS_TARGET] -o cb

where [VERSION] is the cb version and [OS_TARGET] is one of the following reference architectures:

  • Linux: cb-cli-linux-x64
  • Windows: cb-cli-windows-x64.exe
  • Apple Intel: cb-cli-macos-x64
  • Apple M-series: cb-cli-macos-arm64

Example

$ curl -s "https://canarybit-public-binaries.s3.amazonaws.com/?prefix=cb-cli/" | grep -oE '<Key>[^<]+</Key>' | sed -E 's/<\/?Key>//g' | awk -F'/' 'NF>2 {print $2}' | sort -u | awk '{printf "  📁  %s\n", $0}'
  📁  0.2.4
  📁  0.2.5
  📁  0.2.6
  📁  0.3.0

$ curl -fsSL https://canarybit-public-binaries.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/cb-cli/0.3.0/cb-cli-linux-x64 -o cb

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authenticate towards CanaryBit Identity Provider and fetch a valid token for specific CanaryBit services.

Source your credentials (e.g. cb.rc):

cb.rc
export CB_USERNAME=***
export CB_PASSWORD=***

and run:

$ cb login

Display your CanaryBit account information.

$ cb account

Download

docs.title: SIEM integration
docs.text:
Get a snapshot of your IT infrastructure in a SIEM monitoring tool.

The Inspector attestation reports connector allows end-users to easily collect attestation events from CanaryBit Inspector and forward them to a telemetry data collector (e.g. FluentBit). The data collector system can then be connected to a monitoring tool (e.g. Grafana, Splunk, or others) for log aggregation and alerting.

graph LR
    B[Canary Bit Connector] <-.GET.-> A[Canary Bit Inspector] 
    B[Canary Bit Connector] -.-> C[Data Collector] -.-> D[SIEM]
  1. At launch, the Canary Bit Connector locally stores a last_polling file containing the launch timestamp.
  2. At a recurrent schedule, the Canary Bit Connector:
    • reads the last_polling timestamp;
    • fetches the CanaryBit Inspector attestation reports event logs starting from the last_polling timestamp and until the current timestamp;
    • forwards them to the Data Collector for the specific time range.
  3. The last_polling file is then updated with the current timestamp.
  4. The Data Collector is then responsible to forward the event logs to the configured SIEM/monitoring tool.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: • Access to a CanaryBit Inspector instance

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The following variables are required by the connector:

  • CB_USERNAME and CB_PASSWORD for CanaryBit authentication;
  • TELEMETRY_DATA_COLLECTOR_URI for shipping the events to a SIEM monitoring tool.

The connector can then be deployed as either a systemd service or as a container.

Note

We recommend to store the environment variables in an .rc (e.g. my-env.rc)

docs.title: Systemd
docs.text:
1. Create both a .service and .timer file under the systemd directory:

    /etc/systemd/system/connector.service
    [Unit]
Description=CanaryBit Inspector attestation reports connector

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'source my-env.rc && /usr/bin/python3 <PATH>/connector.py
    /etc/systemd/system/connector.timer
    [Unit]
Description=Run the connector daily

[Timer]         
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

  2. Launch the script with: 

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now connector.timer

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
docker run --rm \
  --network <CUSTOM_NETWORK> \
  -e CB_USERNAME \
  -e CB_PASSWORD \
  -e TELEMETRY_DATA_COLLECTOR_URI \
  -v "./last_polling:/app/last_polling" \
  ghcr.io/canarybit/inspector-attestations-connector:latest

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
In this example we use FluentBit and Grafana as telemetry data collector and monitoring tool, respectively.

  1. Create and source a my-env.rc file with the following environment variables:

    export CB_USERNAME=***
export CB_PASSWORD=***

export TELEMETRY_DATA_COLLECTOR_URI=http://fluentbit:9880/attestation.events

export LOKI_HOST=logs-prod-XYZ.grafana.net
export LOKI_USER=***
export LOKI_PASSWORD=***

  2. Configure Loki as FluentBit output plugin:

    [SERVICE]
  Flush         1
  Log_Level     info

[INPUT]
  # ---
  # DO NOT REMOVE !!! 
  # Receives the results from the connector via http          
  # ---
  Name         http
  Listen       0.0.0.0
  Port         9880

[FILTER]
  # ---
  # DO NOT REMOVE !!! 
  # Parses the attestations input and converts it to a multi-line format
  # ---
  Name    lua
  Match   *
  script  /fluent-bit/etc/filter.lua
  call    split_json

[OUTPUT]
  Name          loki
  Match         *
  Host          ${LOKI_HOST}
  Port          443
  tls           On
  tls.verify    On
  http_user     ${LOKI_USER}
  http_passwd   ${LOKI_PASSWORD}
  # ---
  Labels        job=my_attestations
  # ---
  line_format   json

    Info

    Label is used to identify the events and query the results in Grafana. In this example, we used job=my_attestations

  3. Launch FluentBit:

    docker run -d \
  --network my-network \
  --name fluentbit \
  -e LOKI_HOST \
  -e LOKI_USER \
  -e LOKI_PASSWORD \
  -v "$(pwd)/fluent-bit.conf:/fluent-bit/etc/fluent-bit.conf:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/filter.lua:/fluent-bit/etc/filter.lua:ro" \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  fluent/fluent-bit:latest \
  /fluent-bit/bin/fluent-bit -c /fluent-bit/etc/fluent-bit.conf

  4. Launch the connector:

    docker run --rm \
  --network my-network \
  -e CB_USERNAME \
  -e CB_PASSWORD \
  -e TELEMETRY_DATA_COLLECTOR_URI \
  -v "./last_polling:/app/last_polling" \
  ghcr.io/canarybit/inspector-attestations-connector:latest

    Warning

    Make sure that both containers are on the same network, in this example we used my-network.

  5. Visualise the event logs in Grafana

    In Grafana Explore (tab), select the Loki data source connection used to ship the logs to Grafana.

    Run the query selectingjob=my_attestations as Label Filter

    and visualise the return event logs:
